messages.content:
Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
We claim the largest such integer is \(\boxed{1230}\).

First note
\[
450=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2,\qquad 451=11\cdot 41.
\]

## 1. Verify that \(n=1230\) works

We have
\[
\sqrt{1230}\in(35,36),
\]
so
\[
\left\lfloor \sqrt{1230}\right\rfloor=35.
\]
Also
\[
1230=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 41.
\]

We need to show
\[
1230\mid 35!^{1230!}+450.
\]

- For \(p=2,3,5\): since \(p\mid 35!\), we have \(p\mid 35!^{1230!}\). Also \(p\mid 450\). Thus \(p\mid 35!^{1230!}+450\).

- For \(p=41\): since \(41\nmid 35!\), Fermat’s little theorem gives
\[
35!^{40}\equiv 1\pmod{41}.
\]
But \(40\mid 1230!\), so
\[
35!^{1230!}\equiv 1\pmod{41}.
\]
Therefore
\[
35!^{1230!}+450\equiv 1+450=451\equiv 0\pmod{41}.
\]

Since \(1230\) is squarefree, divisibility by \(2,3,5,41\) implies
\[
1230\mid 35!^{1230!}+450.
\]

So \(1230\) is a valid value.

## 2. Show no larger \(n\) can work

Let
\[
k=\left\lfloor \sqrt n\right\rfloor.
\]
If \(k\le 4\), then \(n\le 24<1230\). So assume \(k\ge 5\).

Let \(p\) be any prime divisor of \(n\).

### Case 1: \(p\le k\)

Then \(p\mid k!\), so
\[
k!^{n!}\equiv 0\pmod p.
\]
Since \(n\mid k!^{n!}+450\), we must have
\[
p\mid 450.
\]
Thus \(p\in\{2,3,5\}\).

For \(p\in\{2,3,5\}\), let
\[
b=v_p(450).
\]
Because \(k\ge 5\), we have \(n\ge 25\), so \(n!>2\). Also \(v_p(k!)\ge 1\), hence
\[
v_p(k!^{n!})=n!v_p(k!)>b=v_p(450).
\]
Therefore
\[
v_p(k!^{n!}+450)=v_p(450)=b.
\]
Since \(n\) divides the expression, we get
\[
v_p(n)\le v_p(450).
\]
So
\[
v_2(n)\le 1,\qquad v_3(n)\le 2,\qquad v_5(n)\le 2.
\]

### Case 2: \(p>k\)

Then \(p\nmid k!\), so \(\gcd(k!,p)=1\). Also \(p\mid n\), so \(p-1\mid n!\). Hence by Fermat’s little theorem,
\[
k!^{n!}\equiv 1\pmod p.
\]
Thus
\[
k!^{n!}+450\equiv 451\pmod p.
\]
Since \(p\mid n\), we need
\[
p\mid 451=11\cdot 41.
\]
So any prime divisor of \(n\) larger than \(k\) must be \(11\) or \(41\).

Moreover, if \(p>k\), then \(p\ge k+1\), so
\[
p^2\ge (k+1)^2>(k+1)^2-1\ge n.
\]
Thus \(p^2\nmid n\), and two distinct primes larger than \(k\) cannot both divide \(n\). Therefore \(n\) has at most one prime factor larger than \(k\), and it occurs to the first power.

Therefore \(n\) has the form
\[
n=r t,
\]
where
\[
t\in\{1,11,41\}
\]
and
\[
r=2^a3^b5^c
\]
with
\[
0\le a\le 1,\qquad 0\le b\le 2,\qquad 0\le c\le 2.
\]
In particular,
\[
r\mid 450.
\]

Now bound each possibility:

- If \(t=1\), then \(n=r\le 450\).
- If \(t=11\), then \(11>k\), so \(k\le 10\). Also \(r=n/11\le k\le 10\), so \(n\le 110\).
- If \(t=41\), then \(41>k\), so \(k\le 40\). Also \(r=n/41\le k\le 40\). Since \(r\mid 450\) and \(r\le 40\), the largest possible such \(r\) is \(30\). Hence
  \[
  n=41r\le 41\cdot 30=1230.
  \]

Thus every valid \(n\) satisfies \(n\le 1230\). Since \(1230\) itself works, the largest possible value is

\[
\boxed{1230}.
\]
